content: Through improved implementation of the guidance on estimating requirements for substances under international control, healthcare systems can better ensure the availability of essential medications for palliative care. Collaboration with UNICEF and other relevant partners is critical to promoting and implementing palliative care services specifically tailored for children, addressing their unique needs. Monitoring the global status of palliative care is essential. This involves evaluating progress in various initiatives and programs in partnership with Member States and international organizations. Such efforts help identify gaps and opportunities for improvement in palliative care delivery worldwide. Member States should be encouraged to allocate adequate funding and foster enhanced cooperation for palliative care programs and research initiatives. This is particularly important in resource-limited countries, aligning with the Programme Budget 2014–2015, which emphasizes the importance of palliative care. Research on effective models of palliative care in lowand middle-income countries should be prioritized. These models should incorporate best practices and be adaptable to local contexts to ensure their success and sustainability. A report on the progress of implementing this resolution should be presented to the Sixty-ninth World Health Assembly in 2016, providing a comprehensive overview of advancements and challenges. Palliative care strategic planning should be integrated into healthcare institutions. This includes training healthcare professionals, such as community health workers (CHWs), to deliver palliative care effectively. CHWs should be equipped with knowledge about the medical, psychosocial, and spiritual needs of patients, as well as skills in communication, symptom recognition, and when to seek supervisory support. Resilience and self-care for caregivers, along with grief and bereavement support for families, are essential components of palliative care. These aspects ensure holistic care for both patients and their support systems. Palliative care should focus on alleviating serious health-related suffering (SHS) associated with life-limiting or life-threatening conditions. SHS is defined as suffering that cannot be relieved without medical intervention and significantly impacts physical, social, or emotional functioning. Integrated health services should ensure a continuum of care, including health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care. These services should be accessible at all levels of the healthcare system and tailored to the needs of individuals throughout their life course. Universal health coverage (UHC) must include access to palliative care services, protecting individuals from financial hardship while ensuring the provision of high-quality, effective care. This encompasses health promotion, disease prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, and end-of-life care. Social determinants of health, such as the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age, must be addressed to reduce health inequities. These determinants are shaped by the distribution of money, power, and resources at global, national, and local levels. Hospices play a vital role in providing dedicated inpatient or outpatient palliative care for patients nearing the end of life. These institutions are essential for delivering compassionate and specialized care. Internally displaced persons (IDPs) and refugees face unique challenges in accessing healthcare, including palliative care. IDPs, who remain within their country’s borders, often lack the protections afforded to refugees under international law, making it crucial to address their healthcare needs through targeted interventions. Intersectoral action, involving multiple sectors beyond health, is necessary to design and implement public policies that improve healthcare and quality of life. People-centered health services should incorporate the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities, ensuring that healthcare systems respond to their needs in humane and holistic ways.
